summary: Source decomposition of ES.1's orthogonality identity and of ES.2's mean-value theorem along the decoupling route, from Bourgain-Demeter-Guth arXiv:1512.01565v3: the analytic representation of J_{s,n}(N), the main conjecture in Vinogradov's mean value theorem with both terms and its actual degree scope (n >= 2, not only n >= 4), the sharp l^2 decoupling inequality for the moment curve at the critical exponent n(n+1) with its exact ball radius and weight, the discrete restriction estimate and the well-separated-reals generalization that converts decoupling into the solution count, the ball inflation inequality and the multilinear Kakeya hierarchy it rests on, and the epsilon-removal argument above the critical exponent. The interior of the decoupling proof (the induction on scales and the iteration scheme, printed pp. 10-38) was not read and is recorded as an explicit boundary, as are the quoted Kakeya/Brascamp-Lieb inputs and Wooley's two arc estimates. ES.0 is linked to the finite-field producer FF.2 decomposed elsewhere in EXT-08 but otherwise has no acquired source; ES.3, ES.4 and ES.5 are not read.

nodes.title: Orthogonality identity: the Vinogradov solution count as a torus integral of an exponential sum
nodes.statement: For integers s >= 1 and n, N >= 2 let J_{s,n}(N) be the number of integral solutions of the simultaneous system X_1^i + ... + X_s^i = X_{s+1}^i + ... + X_{2s}^i for 1 <= i <= n with 1 <= X_1,...,X_{2s} <= N. Then J_{s,n}(N) = integral over [0,1]^n of | sum_{j=1}^{N} e(x_1 j + x_2 j^2 + ... + x_n j^n) |^{2s} dx_1...dx_n, where e(z) = e^{2 pi i z}.
hypotheses: The system is the FULL translation-invariant system of n equations, one for each power 1 <= i <= n; dropping any equation changes the count
The 2s variables range over the integers in [1,N]; the identity is exact, with no error term
The integral is over the n-torus [0,1]^n with Lebesgue measure; the exponent is 2s, an even integer, so the integrand is |F|^{2s} and is non-negative
proofSteps: Expand |sum_j e(x . (j, j^2, ..., j^n))|^{2s} as a sum over 2s-tuples (X_1,...,X_{2s}) of e( sum_i x_i (X_1^i + ... + X_s^i - X_{s+1}^i - ... - X_{2s}^i) ).

Integrate term by term over [0,1]^n; by orthogonality of the characters x -> e(x . m) on the torus, the integral of each term is 1 if all n of the differences Z_i = X_1^i + ... + X_s^i - (X_{s+1}^i + ... + X_{2s}^i) vanish and 0 otherwise.
The surviving terms are exactly the solutions counted by J_{s,n}(N).
acceptance: Small-case check: n = 1, s = 1, N = 2 gives J = #{(X_1,X_2) : X_1 = X_2} = 2, matching the integral of |e(x)+e(2x)|^2 over [0,1].
Check that the diagonal solutions X_{s+i} = X_{sigma(i)} always contribute, giving the lower bound J_{s,n}(N) >> N^s which is the first term of the conjectured upper bound.
Check that the count with only the first n-1 equations is strictly larger, so the identity is sensitive to the exact system.

The number J_{s,n}(N) has the following analytic representation J_{s,n}(N) = integral_{[0,1]^n} | sum_{j=1}^N e(x_1 j + x_2 j^2 + ... + x_n j^n) |^{2s} dx_1 ... dx_n.

nodes.title: Theorem 1.1: the main conjecture in Vinogradov's mean value theorem, with both terms and the epsilon loss
nodes.statement: For each s >= 1 and n, N >= 2, J_{s,n}(N) <~ N^{s + epsilon} + N^{2s - n(n+1)/2 + epsilon}, the implied constant depending on n, s and epsilon. The bound is sharp apart from the N^epsilon loss. The statement is proved here for all n >= 2; the case n = 2 follows from elementary divisor-function estimates and the case n = 3 was proved earlier by Wooley by efficient congruencing.
hypotheses: s >= 1 an integer, n >= 2, N >= 2; the implied constant is allowed to depend on n, s and epsilon but not on N
Two terms are asserted; neither dominates for all s. The crossover is at 2s = n(n+1), where both exponents equal s
The epsilon loss is genuinely present in this statement; it is removable only for 2s = p > n(n+1) (see the separate epsilon-removal node)

The lower bound J_{s,n}(N) >> N^s + N^{2s - n(n+1)/2} is classical (diagonal solutions and the volume heuristic) and is what makes the theorem sharp; it is asserted, not proved, in the source ('Apart from the N^epsilon loss, this bound has been known to be sharp')
proofSteps: Reduce to the decoupling inequality Theorem 1.2 for the moment curve Gamma_n, via the discrete restriction estimate Theorem 4.1 and the Schwartz-majorant argument of Corollary 4.2 (see the corresponding nodes).

Theorem 1.2 itself is proved by the three-ingredient scheme described in section 3: multilinear Kakeya-type theorems (Theorem 6.5), the Bourgain-Guth induction on scales relating linear and multilinear decoupling, and an iteration producing the multi-scale inequality of Theorem 8.3.
PROOF-READING BOUNDARY: sections 6 (after Theorem 6.6), 7, 8 and 9 of the source, which contain the actual induction and iteration, were not read for this packet.
acceptance: Degree scope: the title of the source says 'for degrees higher than three', but the theorem as stated covers n >= 2. A consumer must not conclude that low degrees are unproved here: the source says the case n = 2 follows easily from elementary divisor-function estimates and attributes n = 3 to Wooley. ES.2's acceptance condition on low degrees is satisfied by this reading, provided the n = 2 and n = 3 attributions are carried.
Both terms must be stated: a formalization that records only N^{2s - n(n+1)/2 + epsilon} is false for small s.
Check the crossover 2s = n(n+1) numerically for n = 2 (s = 3) and n = 3 (s = 6).
Check that the epsilon is uniform in N but the constant is not uniform in epsilon.

sources.locator: Theorem 1.1 and the surrounding remarks, printed p. 1
sources.excerpt: Theorem 1.1. For each s >= 1 and n, N >= 2 we have the upper bound J_{s,n}(N) . N^{s+epsilon} + N^{2s - n(n+1)/2 + epsilon}. In spite of its name, this result was in fact a conjecture until fairly recently, for n >= 3. The case n = 3 was solved by Wooley in [18] ... The case n = 2 follows easily from elementary estimates for the divisor function. ... The N^epsilon loss in Theorem 1.1 can be removed for p > n(n+1), see (7) below.

nodes.title: Theorem 1.2: the sharp l^2 decoupling inequality for the moment curve at the critical exponent n(n+1)
nodes.statement: Let Gamma = {Phi(t) = (t, t^2, ..., t^n) : 0 <= t <= 1} and for g : [0,1] -> C and an interval J in [0,1] let E_J g(x) = integral_J g(t) e(t x_1 + t^2 x_2 + ... + t^n x_n) dt. Let n >= 2 and 0 < delta <= 1. Then for each ball B in R^n of radius delta^{-n} and each g, ||E_{[0,1]} g||_{L^{n(n+1)}(w_B)} <~_epsilon delta^{-epsilon} ( sum_{J subset [0,1], |J| = delta} ||E_J g||^2_{L^{n(n+1)}(w_B)} )^{1/2}, where w_B(x) = (1 + |x - c_B|/R)^{-100n} for B = B(c_B, R). The implicit constant is independent of delta, B and g.
hypotheses: The ball radius is exactly delta^{-n}, matching the curvature scale of the moment curve at resolution delta; a smaller ball does not suffice
The Lebesgue exponent is exactly the critical n(n+1); the inequality is stated at that exponent only, and other exponents are obtained by Holder and the trivial L^infinity bound

The weight w_B is a polynomial (not exponential) mollification of the indicator of B with exponent 100n; it is what makes the localized norms additive over a finitely overlapping cover (inequality (3))
delta^{-1} is assumed to be an integer and J ranges over the intervals [j delta, (j+1) delta] for 0 <= j <= delta^{-1} - 1
The right-hand side is an l^2 sum over the delta-intervals: this is an l^2 decoupling, not an l^p one
proofSteps: Section 3 of the source lists the three ingredients: (i) multilinear Kakeya-type theorems for families of plates (Theorem 6.5), which become available after passing to a multilinear version of the decoupling inequality; (ii) the Bourgain-Guth induction on scales [12], which shows the linear decoupling is essentially equivalent to its multilinear version and permits a bootstrap driving the decoupling constants to their conjectured values; (iii) an iteration scheme producing the multi-scale inequality of Theorem 8.3, combining L^2 decoupling, lower dimensional decoupling and ball inflation.
The key new inequality is the ball inflation of Theorem 6.6 (see the corresponding node), which enlarges the spatial ball at fixed intervals, enabling a subsequent decoupling into smaller intervals.
PROOF-READING BOUNDARY: only sections 1-6 (through Theorem 6.6) were read; sections 7-9 containing the bootstrap and the iteration were not.
acceptance: Scale check: for a ball of radius delta^{-n} the curve piece Gamma_J over an interval J of length delta is contained in a delta x delta^2 x ... x delta^n box, which is the dual geometry making the exponent n(n+1) critical.
Exponent check: the inequality FAILS at exponents above n(n+1) with the same delta^{-epsilon} loss; the source only claims n(n+1).
Weight check: replacing w_B by the sharp indicator 1_B breaks the cover inequality (3) used in the proof of Theorem 4.1.
l^2 versus l^p check: the right-hand side is an l^2 aggregation; an l^p version with p = n(n+1) would be a different (stronger for p > 2) statement.

For each ball B subset R^n with radius delta^{-n} and each g : [0,1] -> C we have ||E_{[0,1]} g||_{L^{n(n+1)}(w_B)} . delta^{-epsilon} ( sum_{J subset [0,1], |J| = delta} ||E_J g||^2_{L^{n(n+1)}(w_B)} )^{1/2}. The implicit constant is independent of delta, B, g.
sources.match: Verbatim statement with the radius delta^{-n}, the critical exponent n(n+1), the weight and the l^2 aggregation.

nodes.title: Theorem 4.1 and Corollary 4.2: from decoupling to a discrete restriction estimate and to arbitrary well separated reals
nodes.statement: (Theorem 4.1) For 1 <= i <= N let t_i be a point in ((i-1)/N, i/N]. Then for each R >~ N^n, each ball B_R in R^n, each a_i in C and each p >= 2, ( |B_R|^{-1} integral | sum_i a_i e(x_1 t_i + ... + x_n t_i^n) |^p w_{B_R} )^{1/p} <~ ( N^{epsilon} + N^{(1/2)(1 - n(n+1)/p) + epsilon} ) ||a||_{l^2({1,...,N})}, uniformly in N, R and a. (Corollary 4.2) For each i let X_i be a real with i-1 < X_i <= i, put S_X = {X_1,...,X_N}, and let J_{s,n}(S_X) count the tuples in S_X satisfying the system of INEQUALITIES |X_1^i + ... + X_s^i - (X_{s+1}^i + ... + X_{2s}^i)| <= N^{i-n} for 1 <= i <= n. Then J_{s,n}(S_X) <~ N^{s+epsilon} + N^{2s - n(n+1)/2 + epsilon}, uniformly in S_X. Theorem 1.1 is the special case X_i = i.
hypotheses: The points t_i are only assumed to lie one per interval ((i-1)/N, i/N]: they need not be the rationals i/N, and in Corollary 4.2 the X_i need not be integers
R >~ N^n is required so that B_R can be covered by balls of radius N^n, which is the radius at which Theorem 1.2 applies with delta = 1/N

In Corollary 4.2 the exact equalities of Theorem 1.1 are relaxed to the inequalities |Z_i| <= N^{i-n}; for integer X_i and i = n this forces Z_n = 0, and the smaller thresholds for i < n are what recover the exact system
phi is a fixed positive Schwartz function with non-negative Fourier transform satisfying phi-hat(xi) >= 1 for |xi| <~ 1; such a phi exists and is fixed once and for all
proofSteps: Theorem 4.1: by Holder and the trivial L^infinity bound it suffices to treat p = n(n+1). Cover B_R by a finitely overlapping family of balls of radius N^n, use the elementary weight-summation inequality (3) sum_{B_{N^n}} w_{B_{N^n}} <~ w_{B_R}, apply Theorem 1.2 on each such ball with delta = 1/N, and sum.
Apply the resulting inequality to g = (2 tau)^{-1} sum_i a_i 1_{(t_i - tau, t_i + tau)} and let tau -> 0, which turns E_{[0,1]} g into the discrete exponential sum.

Corollary 4.2: with a_i = 1 and Schwartz decay, (2) gives the moment bound (4) for the phi_{N^n}-weighted 2s-th moment. Apply it with t_i = X_i/N and rescale by phi_{N,1}(x) = phi(x_1/N^{n-1}, x_2/N^{n-2}, ..., x_n).

Expanding the 2s-th power and integrating, each 2s-tuple contributes N^{n(n+1)/2} times integral phi_{N,1}(x) e(x_1 Z_1 + ... + x_n Z_n) dx = N^{n^2} phi-hat(N^{n-1} Z_1, N^{n-2} Z_2, ..., Z_n), which is non-negative and is at least N^{n^2} whenever |Z_i| <~ N^{i-n}, i.e. for each of the J_{s,n}(S_X) solutions. Comparing with (4) gives the bound.
acceptance: Check that Corollary 4.2 counts solutions of INEQUALITIES, not equations, and that the thresholds N^{i-n} depend on i; this is the precise sense in which integers can be replaced by well separated reals.

Check the specialization X_i = i recovers Theorem 1.1, using that for integers the inequality |Z_i| <= N^{i-n} < 1 forces Z_i = 0 only when i < n; the i = n case gives |Z_n| <= 1, so the reduction needs the joint system.
Check the positivity of phi-hat: the argument needs every term in the expansion to be non-negative so that the J_{s,n}(S_X) good terms can be isolated from below.
Check the requirement R >~ N^n in Theorem 4.1; a smaller R invalidates the covering step.

sources.excerpt: Corollary 4.2. For each integer s >= 1 and each S_X as above we have that J_{s,n}(S_X) . N^{s+epsilon} + N^{2s - n(n+1)/2 + epsilon}, where the implicit constant does not depend on S_X. ... Recall that this is always positive, and in fact greater than N^{n^2} at least J_{s,n}(S_X) times. It now suffices to use (4).

nodes.title: Theorem 6.6 (ball inflation) and the multilinear Kakeya hierarchy it rests on
nodes.statement: (Theorem 6.1, Bennett-Carbery-Christ-Tao) For k-dimensional subspaces V_j of R^n with orthogonal projections pi_j, the Brascamp-Lieb type constant sup over g_j in L^2(V_j) of || (prod_{j=1}^{m} |g_j o pi_j|)^{1/m} ||_{L^{2n/k}(R^n)} / (prod_j ||g_j||_{L^2(V_j)})^{1/m} is finite if and only if dim(V) <= (n/(km)) sum_{j=1}^m dim(pi_j(V)) for every linear subspace V of R^n. (Theorem 6.5) For M^n families P_j of plates in R^n, each plate P in P_j having k axes of length R^{1/2} spanning V_k(t_P) for some t_P in I_j and the other n-k axes of length R, all contained in a ball of radius 4R, one has the multilinear Kakeya inequality (10) with the loss R^{epsilon}. (Theorem 6.6, ball inflation) Fix 1 <= k <= n-1 and p >= 2n; let B be a ball of radius rho^{-(k+1)} and let B be a finitely overlapping cover of B by balls Delta of radius rho^{-k}. Then inequality (11) holds: the average over Delta in B of the (p/M_n)-th power of the l^2 aggregate of ||E_{J_i} g||_{L^{pk/n}_#(w_Delta)} is bounded, up to rho^{-epsilon}, by the same expression computed on the single larger ball B.
hypotheses: Theorem 6.1 is an if-and-only-if: the transversality condition (8) is necessary as well as sufficient for finiteness of the Brascamp-Lieb constant

In Theorem 6.5 the plates have a prescribed anisotropic shape (k axes of length R^{1/2} spanning the tangent space V_k(t_P), the remaining n-k of length R) and the functions F_j must be of the form sum_P c_P 1_P; the constant depends on epsilon and K but not on R, c_P or P_j

Theorem 6.6 requires p >= 2n and 1 <= k <= n-1, a ball radius exactly rho^{-(k+1)} and a cover by balls of radius rho^{-k}; the intervals J_i are unchanged from left to right, so (11) is NOT itself a decoupling inequality
rho < 1/K where K is the transversality parameter of the multilinear setup
proofSteps: Theorem 6.1 is quoted from [2] (Bennett, Carbery, Christ, Tao, Math. Res. Lett. 17 (2010)); no proof is given in the source.

Theorem 6.5 is deduced from the Kakeya hierarchy; the source notes that a short proof of the case k = n-1 is in [15] (Guth, Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. 158 (2015)) and that it extends easily to the other values of k, and refers to [8] for further discussion. No proof is written out.

Theorem 6.6's proof begins by reducing, at the cost of logarithmic losses in rho, to families of intervals J_i for which the norms ||E_{J_i} g||_{L^{pk/n}_#(w_B)} have comparable size, dealing with the small ones by the triangle inequality.

The role of (11) in the whole argument is stated in section 3: it is the key new inequality, the 'ball inflation', which enlarges the spatial ball and thereby permits a subsequent decoupling into smaller intervals, each scale corresponding to a particular member of the hierarchy of Theorem 6.5.
PROOF-READING BOUNDARY: the remainder of the proof of Theorem 6.6, and Theorems 6.2-6.4, were not read.
acceptance: Transversality check: verify condition (8) in the concrete configuration used, i.e. for the tangent spaces V_k(t) of the moment curve at K-separated parameters; the k = 1 case is the classical multilinear Kakeya of Bennett-Carbery-Tao.
Radius bookkeeping: in (11) the radii rho^{-k} and rho^{-(k+1)} differ by one power of rho; check that the exponent matches the dimension k of the subspaces used.
Check that (11) leaves the intervals J_i fixed; a reader who mistakes it for a decoupling inequality will misattribute the gain.
Imported-result check: Theorems 6.1 and 6.5 are quoted from [2] and [15] and are not proved here.

sources.locator: Theorem 6.1 with condition (8), Theorem 6.5 with (10), Theorem 6.6 with (11), printed pp. 6-10
sources.excerpt: Theorem 6.6. Fix 1 <= k <= n-1 and p >= 2n. Let B be an arbitrary ball in R^n with radius rho^{-(k+1)}, and let B be a finitely overlapping cover of B with balls Delta of radius rho^{-k}. ... Note that (11) is not a decoupling inequality, as the intervals J_i remain unchanged from left to right. However, the ball on the right is larger, which will allow for subsequent decouplings into smaller intervals.
sources.match: Gives the exact hypotheses of the ball inflation inequality and the source's own explanation of its role, plus the two imported Kakeya/Brascamp-Lieb inputs.

nodes.title: Section 5: removal of the N^epsilon loss for p > n(n+1) via a major/minor arc split
nodes.statement: Let F(x;N) = sum_{j=1}^{N} e(x_1 j + x_2 j^2 + ... + x_n j^n), let L = N^{1/(2n)}, and for 1 <= q <= L and 1 <= a_j <= q with gcd(q, a_1,...,a_n) = 1 define the major arc M(q,a) = {x in [0,1)^n : |x_j - a_j/q| <= L N^{-j}, 1 <= j <= n}; let M be their union and m = [0,1)^n \ M. Assume the two estimates (5) sup_{x in m} |F(x;N)| <~ N^{beta} for some beta < 1 and (6) integral_M |F(x;N)|^p dx <~ N^{p - n(n+1)/2} for p > n(n+1). Then for every fixed p > n(n+1), integral_{[0,1]^n} |F(x;N)|^p dx <~ N^{p - n(n+1)/2}, with NO epsilon loss.
hypotheses: p > n(n+1) strictly; at p = n(n+1) the argument does not apply and the epsilon loss remains
L = N^{1/(2n)} fixes the width of the major arcs; a different L changes both (5) and (6)
The coprimality is joint: gcd(q, a_1, ..., a_n) = 1, not gcd(q,a_j) = 1 for each j

IMPORT STATUS: both (5) and (6) are quoted from Section 7 of Wooley, 'Discrete Fourier restriction via efficient congruencing: basic principles', arXiv:1508.05329 ((6) is his Lemma 7.1); neither is proved in the source read
proofSteps: On the minor arcs, interpolate: integral_m |F|^p <= (sup_m |F|)^{p - n(n+1)} integral_m |F|^{n(n+1)} <~ N^{beta(p - n(n+1))} . N^{n(n+1) - n(n+1)/2 + epsilon}, using (5) for the sup and Theorem 1.1 with 2s = n(n+1) for the remaining integral.

Since beta < 1 is fixed and p > n(n+1) is fixed, the factor N^{beta(p-n(n+1))} is smaller than N^{p - n(n+1)} by a fixed positive power, which absorbs the N^{epsilon} for epsilon small enough; hence integral_m |F|^p <~ N^{p - n(n+1)/2}.
Add the major-arc bound (6) to obtain (7).
acceptance: Check the absorption step explicitly: it needs (1 - beta)(p - n(n+1)) > epsilon, so epsilon must be chosen after p and beta. This is exactly why the removal fails at p = n(n+1).
Check that the major arcs are disjoint for L = N^{1/(2n)} (this is part of ES.1's 'disjointness/overlap control' and is not verified in the source read).
Check the exponent p - n(n+1)/2 against the heuristic: the major arcs contribute the singular series times the singular integral, of order N^{p - n(n+1)/2}.
Check that this node's conclusion is about the exact moment integral, i.e. about J_{s,n}(N) with 2s = p, so p must be an even integer for the count interpretation.

The only ES.0-relevant material decomposed anywhere in EXT-08 is the finite-field input FF.2 (Deligne's Proposition 3.8), recorded as a link here.

The orthogonality identity for the Vinogradov system is decomposed. Not read: disjointness/overlap control of the major arcs M(q,a) for L = N^{1/(2n)} (used in the epsilon-removal node but not proved in the source read), smoothed and weighted variants of the counting identity, and the general major/minor arc apparatus of the circle method, which needs VAUGHAN.

Sections 6 (after Theorem 6.6), 7, 8 and 9 of the source -- the multilinear-to-linear induction on scales, the iteration scheme, Theorem 8.3, and the Appendix -- were NOT read. These contain the actual proof of Theorem 1.2.
Theorem 6.1 is quoted from Bennett-Carbery-Christ-Tao [2] and Theorem 6.5 from Guth [15]; neither was read.
The two estimates (5) and (6) used for epsilon removal are quoted from Wooley arXiv:1508.05329 section 7; not read.
The efficient-congruencing route (Wooley) named as an alternative in ES.2's own text was not read at all; only the decoupling route.
The classical lower bound J_{s,n}(N) >> N^s + N^{2s - n(n+1)/2}, which makes the theorem sharp, is asserted in the source without proof and was not verified.

Singular integrals, p-adic local densities, absolute convergence, factorization and positivity: no source read. Note that the major-arc estimate (6) used in the epsilon-removal node is an L^p bound imported from Wooley, NOT a singular-series computation, so nothing in this packet supplies ES.3.

Waring-type theorems, sums of primes, forms in many variables: no source read. ES.4's own text already warns that the unweighted Vinogradov mean value theorem does not supply the prime-weighted bounds; nothing in this packet changes that.
Determinant method and geometric point counting: no source read.

gaps.title: Degree scope of the decoupling source versus ES.2's acceptance condition
gaps.detail: ES.2's acceptance condition says 'do not cite a degree-greater-than-three source for unproved low-degree cases'. Checked against the source: Theorem 1.1 is stated and proved for all n >= 2 and s >= 1; the phrase 'for degrees higher than three' in the title refers to what was NEW, not to the scope of the theorem. The source adds that the n = 2 case 'follows easily from elementary estimates for the divisor function' (not proved there) and attributes n = 3 to Wooley [18]. So the acceptance condition is satisfiable from this source for n >= 4 directly and for n = 2, 3 only by carrying the two attributions. Recorded so that a consumer does not either over- or under-claim the degree range.
